title: How are you all making trailers for your games? Mine keep falling flat
author: W3103_
selftext:
So my game’s at the point where I’m actually happy with how it looks, and I reckon it’s good enough to get a trailer out. Problem is every trailer I’ve tried to make has come out kind of shitty

I’ve got a couple of ideas for what I want it to look like, but I’ve got no video skills at all. What I’ve been doing is telling the AI “make me a trailer where this happens, then this, show off these shots” and it spits out a worse version of what’s in my head every time.

So how are you all doing it? Is it mostly just gameplay footage cut together? Are people making proper cinematic bits just for the trailer? Doing it in an editor, using AI, recording in-engine?

Would love to hear how others are going about it, because I’m clearly doing something wrong lol

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body:
Once you teach the AI to control and play your game and it can spit out trailers for you in with FFMPEG. To get better control of it, ask to do a storyboard and plan it out shot by shot. How long you want it to be, what parts of the game you want it to show. As it specifically about timing and tell it what you do and don't like.

Here are a few I made. These were produced as stills and made into video, the last one just has music provided by youtube. But all prompt driven, edited by the LLM from screenshots it produced.

comments.author: AlgaeNo3373
comments.body:
I'm currently using the game itself (Godot engine) for most trailers and associated content and liking the results so far even early on. I've tried a few different things from general "smooth pans over scenes" to showcase adding stuff, through to fully-scripted out scenes with bespoke assets and VA etc. Still very early days so none of it looks amazing, but the process itself works well - it's visually consistent with the game because it *is* the game, it's easy to iterate/prototype/polish, and it's faster to capture than it is to render (Godot has a frame-by-frame movie maker mode but that's very slow, I don't use that much). 

Example of a flyby video: [Lunarpunk concepts](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kW0VCcTsyYg)

Example of a scripted cutscene type thing: [Night Call](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ydjYvbpnIV8)

The first is cut together by me in video editor, just to sync with music a bit, but the second is put together by Claude. The second is pretty basic I realize, but it's a first iteration. There's a term called "blocking" where you kinda do the basic version of the scene first at low-poly/quality to get pacing, position, and other things right before going whole hog. This is mostly in that "blocking" sense. 

Elevenlabs is good for SFX generally - but my game already has soundscapes that feed trails, mostly. Don't usually make bespoke stuff unless its for the scripted scenes like "night call" vid. Each trailer uses backing music by Suno. 

Another advance of this approach: in-game cutscenes. The same thing that drives trailers you record, can drive in-game set pieces too. I've been using it for that the last few days to build an intro scene and it's coming along nicely :D
